opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the thing people overlook is that it's not really about one magic trick. From the outside it looks like "oh, you just trained a model to do math," but a lot of the work is in the unglamorous stuff: getting the data right, figuring out what good reasoning traces even look like, and making sure the model can actually write a full, rigorous proof rather than just landing on a final answer.

IMO problems are very different from the benchmark-style math people usually optimize for. There's often no single numeric answer you can check. You have to produce a complete argument that a human grader would accept, and that changes everything about how you evaluate progress. If your eval is noisy or you're grading the wrong thing, you can fool yourself very easily into thinking you're improving when you're not.

The other thing is that it's a bit of a stress test for general capability. You want the model to explore, try different approaches, backtrack when something doesn't work, and verify its own steps, all while staying coherent over a really long chain of reasoning. Getting that behavior to be robust, not just on a handful of cherry-picked problems but consistently, is where a lot of the effort goes.

And then there's the human side: the coordination, the late nights, people checking proofs by hand. It's very much a team sport. The final result looks clean, but the path to it is pretty messy.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts IMO problems with benchmark-style math, but does not describe repeatedly rerunning benchmarks to improve performance versus the IMO unfolding as a live competition.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing people underestimate is how much of it is not about the math at all. Everyone talks about the model's reasoning ability, and sure, that matters, but when you actually sit down to prep a model for something like the IMO, the bottlenecks are way more mundane than that.

The first one is verification. The IMO isn't multiple choice, it's proofs. So you can't just check a final answer against a key, you need some way of knowing whether a long chain of natural-language reasoning is actually correct, with no gaps. That is really hard to do at scale. If your training signal is noisy, you're basically teaching the model to write things that look like proofs rather than things that are proofs, and those two things diverge in very subtle ways. A lot of the real work is building a grading pipeline you actually trust, and honestly, humans disagree with each other on partial credit too, so even your ground truth is fuzzy.

The second one is data contamination, and it's sneakier than people think. Old IMO problems are everywhere on the internet, in forums, in solution books, in blog posts. Even if you deduplicate the exact problems, there are near-duplicates, restatements, problems that are isomorphic to a known one with the numbers changed. So you can get a model that looks great on a held-out set and it's actually just pattern matching to something it's seen. You have to be kind of paranoid about this, and you need genuinely fresh problems to evaluate on, which are scarce and expensive.

Then there's the inference-side stuff. The competition has a time limit. If your model needs to think for hours and sample a thousand times and run a tournament over candidates to get a good proof, is that really the same as solving it? Deciding what compute budget is fair, and then making the model actually work within that budget, is a real engineering problem and it shapes how you train.

And maybe the most overlooked thing is the failure mode where the model doesn't know when to stop. Humans at the IMO are very good at saying, I'm going to abandon this approach, it's not going anywhere. Models tend to keep digging into a dead end, or they convince themselves they've finished when they haven't. Teaching a model to give up on a bad path, or to say honestly "I couldn't do this one," is almost harder than teaching it to solve problems. And it's really important, because a confident wrong proof is worse than no proof.

So yeah, I'd say the math is the glamorous part, and the unglamorous parts, grading, data hygiene, compute budgets, calibration, are where most of the time actually goes.

r001.rationale: The response notes the IMO has a time limit and questions using hours of thought or many samples, but it does not contrast repeatedly rerunning benchmarks to improve performance with the IMO as a live competition.

astra-6.text:
I think people focus on whether the model can find the key mathematical insight, but an easily overlooked part is whether it can turn that insight into a complete, rigorous proof. Those are different capabilities. You can have the right idea and still leave a gap that invalidates the solution.

That also makes evaluation really important. If your training signal rewards proofs that sound convincing but aren’t actually correct, you can improve the wrong thing. So preparing a model for the IMO is partly about teaching it to explore, but also about teaching it to check its own work, recognize an unjustified step, and go back rather than confidently finish.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people focus a lot on the model’s mathematical ability, but the evaluation setup is easy to overlook. What does it actually mean to sit the IMO? How much time does the model get? Can it use tools? Does it have to produce a complete proof, and who judges whether that proof is valid?

Those details matter because having the right idea is very different from writing a proof that earns full marks. A model can make a plausible argument and quietly skip the hardest step. So preparing it isn’t just about teaching it more mathematics. It’s also about getting it to check its own reasoning, recognize gaps, and use its time well under the actual competition constraints.

r001.rationale: The response discusses competition constraints and using time well, but it does not contrast repeatedly rerunning benchmarks to improve performance with the IMO as a live competition.
